words.meaning: born of birth, herbs, mantra, austerity or absorption

translations.text: The perfections are born of birth, herbs, mantra, austerity or absorption.

notes: Vyāsa: by birth: the perfection that belongs to another body. By herbs: by the elixir, in the dwellings of the asuras, and the like. By mantra: moving through space, minuteness and the rest. By austerity: the fulfilment of intention; he takes what form he wishes and goes where he wishes. Those born of absorption have been explained.

words.meaning: the change into another kind of birth
from the filling in of the natures

translations.text: The change into another kind of birth comes from the filling in of the natures.

notes: Vyāsa: when body and senses change into another kind, the earlier form passes and the later arises by the entering of parts not there before. The natures (prakṛti), the material causes of body and senses, favour each its own modification by filling in, depending on a cause such as dharma.

sanskrit.iast: nimittam aprayojakaṃ prakṛtīnāṃ varaṇabhedas tu tataḥ kṣetrikavat || 3 ||

lines.iast: nimittam aprayojakaṃ prakṛtīnāṃ varaṇabhedas tu tataḥ kṣetrikavat

padaccheda.iast: nimittam aprayojakam prakṛtīnām varaṇa-bhedaḥ tu tataḥ kṣetrika-vat
padaccheda.deva: निमित्तम् अप्रयोजकम् प्रकृतीनाम् वरण-भेदः तु ततः क्षेत्रिक-वत्

translations.text: The occasioning cause does not set the natures in motion; from it comes only the breaking of the barrier, as with a farmer.

notes: Vyāsa: a cause such as dharma does not move the natures, for a cause is not moved by its effect. As a farmer who wants to flood a field from one full of water does not carry the water with his hands but breaks the bank, and the water flows of itself; so dharma breaks adharma, the barrier of the natures, and they flow of themselves each into its own modification. Or as the farmer cannot push the sap into the roots of the rice but pulls out the weeds, and the sap enters of itself. So dharma is the cause only of the ceasing of adharma. Nandīśvara and others are examples; and in reverse, where adharma overcomes dharma, Nahuṣa the serpent and others.

words.meaning: from the bare sense of ‘I am’

translations.text: Created minds come from the bare sense of ‘I am’.

notes: Vyāsa: when the yogin creates many bodies, do they have one mind or many? Taking the bare sense of ‘I am’, the cause of mind, he makes created minds; so the bodies have minds.

translations.text: In their different activities one mind is the mover of the many.

notes: Vyāsa: how do many minds act according to the purpose of one? He creates one mind that moves them all.

translations.text: Of these, the one born of meditation is without a store.

notes: Vyāsa: the created mind is of five kinds, as the perfections are. Only the mind born of meditation has no store, no activity of attachment and the like, and so no tie with merit and evil, for the yogin's afflictions have wasted away. The others have a store of action.

translations.text: The yogin's action is neither white nor black; that of others is of three kinds.

notes: Vyāsa: action is of four classes. Black is that of the wicked. White-and-black is done by outer means, and its store is heaped up by hurting or helping others. White belongs to those given to austerity, recitation and meditation: it depends on the mind alone and hurts no one. Neither white nor black is that of renouncers whose afflictions have wasted away, in their last body: not white because the yogin renounces its fruit, not black because he does not take it up.

words.meaning: of those that accord with its ripening

translations.text: From that comes the manifestation of only those latent tendencies that accord with its ripening.

notes: Vyāsa: from the threefold action. Action that ripens as a god's life cannot bring out the tendencies of a being in hell, an animal or a man, but only those that accord with a god's; and so for the others.

words.meaning: of those separated by birth, place and time
because they are of one form

translations.text: Even when they are separated by birth, place and time there is unbroken succession, because memory and latent impression are of one form.

notes: Vyāsa: the ripening as a cat, if it rises again after a hundred births, a great distance or a hundred ages, rises at once with the tendencies formed by the earlier life as a cat, when like action brings it out. As the experiences, so the impressions; as the tendencies, so the memory. Since the relation of cause and effect is not cut, there is succession even across the gap.

translations.text: And they are without beginning, because the wish is constant.

notes: Vyāsa: the wish for oneself, ‘may I not cease to be; may I be’, is seen in all. It is not natural: how could a creature just born, which has not known death, fear it? So this mind, pierced by beginningless tendencies, takes up some of them as a cause prompts, for the Puruṣa's experience. Others hold that the mind shrinks and spreads to the size of the body, like a lamp in a pot or a palace; the teacher holds that the mind is all-pervading and only its activity shrinks and spreads. That depends on causes: outer, needing the body (praise, giving, salutation), and inner, of the mind alone (faith and the like). The mental is the stronger.

words.meaning: by cause, fruit, substrate and support

translations.text: Because they are held together by cause, fruit, substrate and support, in the absence of these they too are absent.

notes: Vyāsa: the cause: from dharma pleasure, from adharma pain; from pleasure attachment, from pain aversion; from these effort, by which one helps or harms another with mind, speech or body; and from that again dharma and adharma. So turns the six-spoked wheel of the cycle of birth and death, and its driver is ignorance, the root of all afflictions. The fruit is that for the sake of which dharma and the like arise. The substrate is the mind that still has a task. The support is the thing which, when present, brings a tendency out.

words.meaning: because of the difference of the paths of time

translations.text: The past and the future exist in their own form; the properties differ by their path of time.

notes: Vyāsa: he asks how the tendencies, existing as real, can cease, since nothing arises from the non-existent and nothing existent perishes. The future is what is yet to be manifest, the past what has been manifest, the present what is at work; all three are objects of knowledge, and knowledge without an object would not arise. A cause can make an existing fruit present; it cannot produce what was not. Past and future do not exist as the present does, as a manifest thing; the future exists in its own form to be manifested, the past in its own form as having been manifested.

words.meaning: have the guṇas as their nature

translations.text: They are manifest or subtle, and have the guṇas as their nature.

notes: Vyāsa: the present ones are manifest; the past and future ones are subtle, of the form of the six unparticulars. All this is only a particular arrangement of the guṇas. So the teaching says: ‘The highest form of the guṇas does not come within sight; what comes within sight is like illusion, of little worth.’

words.meaning: from the oneness of the change

translations.text: The reality of a thing comes from the oneness of the change.

notes: Vyāsa: if all is the guṇas, how is there one sound, one sense? The guṇas as means of grasping have one change, the sense of hearing; as what is grasped they have one change, sound; the subtle elements have one change, the atom of earth; and these one change, the earth, a cow, a tree. Those who say that there is no object apart from cognition, that a thing is only constructed by knowledge, like a dream object, deny the thing as it presents itself by its own power; how should they be believed?

grammar.en: past passive participle m. nom. sg.

translations.text: The thing being the same and minds differing, the paths of the two are separate.

notes: Vyāsa: one thing is the common object of many minds; it is not constructed by one mind or by many, but stands in itself. Of the same thing one mind has a pleasant cognition through dharma, another a painful one through adharma, another a deluded one through ignorance, another a neutral one through right seeing. So thing and knowledge, the grasped and the grasping, go separate ways.

sanskrit.deva: न चैकचित्ततन्त्रं वस्तु तदप्रमाणकं तदा किं स्यात् ॥ १६ ॥
sanskrit.iast: na caikacittatantraṃ vastu tadapramāṇakaṃ tadā kiṃ syāt || 16 ||

lines.iast: na caikacittatantraṃ vastu tadapramāṇakaṃ tadā kiṃ syāt
lines.deva: न चैकचित्ततन्त्रं वस्तु तदप्रमाणकं तदा किं स्यात्

padaccheda.iast: na ca eka-citta-tantram vastu tat apramāṇakam tadā kim syāt
padaccheda.deva: न च एक-चित्त-तन्त्रम् वस्तु तत् अप्रमाणकम् तदा किम् स्यात्

translations.text: And a thing does not depend on one mind; when not known by that mind, what would it then be?

notes: Vyāsa: if a thing depended on one mind, then when that mind was distracted or had ceased, the thing, untouched by it and not the object of another, would be nothing at all; and whence would it arise again? The parts of it not present to the mind would not exist: there being no back, there would be no belly either. So the object is independent and common to all Puruṣas, and minds are independent, one for each Puruṣa. From the relation of the two comes perception, which is the Puruṣa's experience.

words.meaning: because it depends on being coloured by that

translations.text: A thing is known or unknown to the mind according as the mind is coloured by it.

notes: Vyāsa: objects are like magnets; the mind, like iron, is drawn and coloured by them. The object that colours it is known, another is unknown. Since its object is now known and now unknown, the mind is subject to change.

padaccheda.iast: sadā jñātāḥ citta-vṛttayaḥ tat-prabhoḥ puruṣasya apariṇāmitvāt
padaccheda.deva: सदा ज्ञाताः चित्त-वृत्तयः तत्-प्रभोः पुरुषस्य अपरिणामित्वात्

grammar.en: past passive participle f. nom. pl.

translations.text: The activities of the mind are always known, because its lord, the Puruṣa, does not change.

notes: Vyāsa: if the Puruṣa, the lord, changed as the mind does, the mind's activities, his objects, would be now known and now unknown, like sound and other objects. That the mind is always known lets one infer that the Puruṣa does not change.

translations.text: It is not self-illuminating, because it is something seen.

notes: Vyāsa: lest it be thought that the mind lights up both itself and its object, like fire. As the senses and sound and the rest are not self-illuminating, being seen, so the mind. Fire is no example: fire does not light up a self that was unlit, and light is seen where what lights and what is lit are joined; there is no such joining in a thing's own form alone. And beings are seen to be aware of the movement of their own understanding: ‘I am angry, I am afraid’.

words.meaning: there is no ascertaining of both

translations.text: And both cannot be ascertained at one time.

notes: Vyāsa: it is not possible to ascertain one's own form and another's in a single moment. For the holder of momentariness, a thing's coming to be is itself the act and the agent.

words.meaning: if it were seen by another mind

translations.text: If it were seen by another mind, there would be an endless regress of cognition of cognition, and confusion of memories.

notes: Vyāsa: if a mind were grasped by the next mind, by what is that cognition grasped? By another, and that by another. And there would be as many memories as cognitions of cognitions, so that no single memory could be ascertained. Those who deny the Puruṣa, who is aware of the understanding, have thrown everything into confusion. The Sāṃkhya, Yoga and like teachings mean by the word ‘own’ the Puruṣa, the owner and experiencer of the mind.

words.meaning: which does not pass over (into objects)
when it takes on its form
the awareness of its own understanding

translations.text: Consciousness, which does not pass over into objects, is aware of its own understanding when that takes on its form.

notes: Vyāsa: the power of the experiencer does not change or pass over; it seems to have passed into the changing object and follows its activity. Because it merely imitates the activity of the understanding that has received the tinge of consciousness, the activity of knowing is said to be not distinct from that of the understanding.

words.meaning: coloured by the seer and the seen

translations.text: The mind, coloured by the seer and the seen, has all for its object.

notes: Vyāsa: the mind is coloured by the object thought of, and, being itself an object, is tied to the Puruṣa, the subject. So it appears as object and subject, as conscious and unconscious, like a crystal. Misled by this likeness some call the mind itself conscious; others say that all this is mind only and there is no world of cows and pots. They are to be pitied. In the wisdom of absorption the object is reflected and is other than the wisdom; that by which the reflected object is ascertained in wisdom is the Puruṣa. Those who separate grasper, grasping and grasped as three kinds see rightly.

sanskrit.iast: tad asaṃkhyeyavāsanābhiś citram api parārthaṃ saṃhatyakāritvāt || 24 ||

lines.iast: tad asaṃkhyeyavāsanābhiś citram api parārthaṃ saṃhatyakāritvāt

padaccheda.iast: tat asaṃkhyeya-vāsanābhiḥ citram api para-artham saṃhatya-kāritvāt
padaccheda.deva: तत् असंख्येय-वासनाभिः चित्रम् अपि पर-अर्थम् संहत्य-कारित्वात्

translations.text: Though variegated by countless latent tendencies, it exists for another, because it works by combining.

notes: Vyāsa: for the experience and liberation of another, not for itself, like a house. A pleasant mind is not for the sake of pleasure, nor knowledge for the sake of knowledge. The other is the Puruṣa, who has experience and liberation as his purpose; he does not work by combining.

words.meaning: for one who sees the distinction
the ceasing of reflection on his own state

translations.text: For one who sees the distinction, reflection on his own state ceases.

notes: Vyāsa: as the sprouting of grass in the rains shows that its seed was there, so in one whose hair stands on end and whose tears fall on hearing of the path of release, a seed of seeing the distinction is inferred. In him the reflection arises naturally: ‘Who was I? How was I? What is this? What shall we be?’ It ceases for one who sees the distinction: this varied change belongs to the mind alone; the Puruṣa, when ignorance is gone, is pure and untouched by the mind's properties.

translations.text: Then the mind slopes towards discernment and is borne on towards soleness.

notes: Vyāsa: his mind, which was borne towards objects and sloped towards ignorance, becomes otherwise.

translations.text: In the gaps of that, other cognitions arise from latent impressions.

notes: Vyāsa: in the mind that flows only with the vision of the difference of sattva and the Puruṣa, ‘I am’, ‘mine’, ‘I know’, ‘I do not know’ arise in the gaps, from earlier impressions whose seeds are wasting away.

grammar.en: past passive participle n. nom. sg.

translations.text: Their avoidance is said to be like that of the afflictions.

notes: Vyāsa: as the afflictions, become like burnt seeds, cannot sprout, so the earlier impression, burnt by the fire of knowledge, bears no cognition. The impressions of knowledge last until the mind's task is ended, so they need no thought.

sanskrit.iast: prasaṃkhyāne 'py akusīdasya sarvathā vivekakhyāter dharmameghaḥ samādhiḥ || 29 ||

lines.iast: prasaṃkhyāne 'py akusīdasya sarvathā vivekakhyāter dharmameghaḥ samādhiḥ

padaccheda.iast: prasaṃkhyāne api akusīdasya sarvathā viveka-khyāteḥ dharma-meghaḥ samādhiḥ
padaccheda.deva: प्रसंख्याने अपि अकुसीदस्य सर्वथा विवेक-ख्यातेः धर्म-मेघः समाधिः

words.meaning: for one who seeks no gain

translations.text: For one who seeks no gain even in reflection, from the vision of discernment in every way there comes the absorption called the ‘cloud of dharma’.

notes: Vyāsa: when he wants nothing even from reflection and is dispassionate towards that too, there is only the vision of discernment at all times; the seeds of impressions having wasted away, no other cognitions arise.

words.meaning: the ceasing of afflictions and actions

translations.text: From that, afflictions and actions cease.

notes: Vyāsa: the afflictions, ignorance and the rest, are torn up by the root, and the stores of good and bad action are destroyed with their root. When these have ceased the knower is liberated while still living; for error is the cause of birth, and no one whose error has wasted away is seen to be born.

padaccheda.iast: tadā sarva-āvaraṇa-mala-apetasya jñānasya ānantyāt jñeyam alpam
padaccheda.deva: तदा सर्व-आवरण-मल-अपेतस्य ज्ञानस्य आनन्त्यात् ज्ञेयम् अल्पम्

words.meaning: freed from all the stains that cover it

translations.text: Then, because knowledge freed from all the stains that cover it is infinite, what is to be known is little.

notes: Vyāsa: the sattva of knowledge is infinite; covered by tamas, it is uncovered only here and there by rajas. Freed of all covering it is infinite, and what is to be known becomes little, like a firefly in the sky.

words.meaning: the end of the sequence of changes

translations.text: From that, the sequence of changes of the guṇas, their purpose accomplished, comes to an end.

notes: Vyāsa: from the rise of the cloud of dharma. Having brought about experience and liberation, they cannot stay even a moment.

words.meaning: to be grasped at the end of a change

translations.text: Sequence is correlated with the moments and is grasped at the end of a change.

notes: Vyāsa: a cloth is not old at the end without having passed through the sequence of moments. Sequence is seen in eternal things too. Eternity is of two kinds: the unchanging eternity of the Puruṣa and the changing eternity of the guṇas; that is eternal whose essence is not destroyed while it changes. In the properties of the guṇas, the understanding and the rest, the sequence has an end; in the guṇas themselves it has none.

Vyāsa: does the sequence of the cycle of birth and death end or not? This cannot be answered outright. ‘Will all who are born die?’ can be answered so: yes. ‘Will all who die be born?’ needs a division: the skilled one, in whom the vision has arisen and thirst has wasted away, will not; another will. So here: for the skilled one the cycle ends, for another it does not.

sanskrit.deva: पुरुषार्थशून्यानां गुणानां प्रतिप्रसवः कैवल्यं स्वरूपप्रतिष्ठा वा चितिशक्तिरिति ॥ ३४ ॥
sanskrit.iast: puruṣārthaśūnyānāṃ guṇānāṃ pratiprasavaḥ kaivalyaṃ svarūpapratiṣṭhā vā citiśaktir iti || 34 ||

lines.iast: puruṣārthaśūnyānāṃ guṇānāṃ pratiprasavaḥ kaivalyaṃ svarūpapratiṣṭhā vā citiśaktir iti
lines.deva: पुरुषार्थशून्यानां गुणानां प्रतिप्रसवः कैवल्यं स्वरूपप्रतिष्ठा वा चितिशक्तिरिति

padaccheda.iast: puruṣa-artha-śūnyānām guṇānām pratiprasavaḥ kaivalyam svarūpa-pratiṣṭhā vā citi-śaktiḥ iti
padaccheda.deva: पुरुष-अर्थ-शून्यानाम् गुणानाम् प्रतिप्रसवः कैवल्यम् स्वरूप-प्रतिष्ठा वा चिति-शक्तिः इति

words.meaning: empty of any purpose for the Puruṣa

translations.text: Soleness is the return to their source of the guṇas, empty of any purpose for the Puruṣa; or it is the power of consciousness resting in its own nature.

notes: Vyāsa: the return to their source of the guṇas, as effects and causes, when experience and liberation are accomplished. Or: the Puruṣa's power of consciousness, alone, no longer tied to the sattva of the understanding; its abiding so for ever is soleness.
